explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Isaiah says righteousness once resided in her, "…but now only murderers!" (Isaiah 1:21). I think this is a heavy line, and it's okay to let it sit heavy. The city went from full of justice to that.

The verse never mentions foreigners, friend. Isaiah says the city that once had righteousness living in her now has "only murderers!" (Isaiah 1:21). The problem he describes is inside the city itself. I think this one is a heavy line, so take your time with it.

Beggars never come up in this verse, friend. Isaiah says that where righteousness once resided, there are now "only murderers!" (Isaiah 1:21). I think that's a heavy thing to read, and it's good to slow down for it. The text names murderers, so that's the answer.

Water it is. Isaiah says, "your fine wine is diluted with water." (Isaiah 1:22). Picture me stretching one chocolate chip across an entire batch of cookies. Folks would notice, and I'd be the one blushing at the counter.

Honey would at least be sweet, friend, but that's not what the verse says. Isaiah says the fine wine "…is diluted with water." (Isaiah 1:22). Something good got thinned out until it wasn't so good anymore. Water is the answer.

Oil doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The text says, "your fine wine is diluted with water." (Isaiah 1:22). Fine wine is the good stuff, and it got watered down. Think of a cookie that's all dough and no chips, and you've got the idea.

You got it, baker. Isaiah says, "They all love bribes and chasing after rewards." (Isaiah 1:23). Rulers are supposed to listen to the people in front of them. These rulers were busy listening for the next payoff.

Isaiah doesn't mention feasts or robes here, friend. He says the rulers "…all love bribes and chasing after rewards." (Isaiah 1:23). Their love was for what they could get out of the job. Bribes and rewards are the answer.

Towers and walls aren't in this verse, friend. Isaiah says the rulers "…all love bribes and chasing after rewards." (Isaiah 1:23). That's a love of payoffs, not of building. I'd stick with bribes and rewards.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says the rulers "…do not defend the fatherless…" (Isaiah 1:23). God had told His people to defend them (Isaiah 1:17), and the rulers weren't doing it. So the answer is False.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says the rulers "…do not defend the fatherless…" (Isaiah 1:23). God had told His people to defend them (Isaiah 1:17), so this is the opposite of what He asked. The rulers weren't doing what they were supposed to do.

Yes, friend. The Lord GOD of Hosts says, "…avenge Myself on My enemies." (Isaiah 1:24). He says it right alongside being relieved of His foes. It's a serious declaration, and the text lets it stand as it is.
That's not what He says, friend. The Lord GOD of Hosts declares, "…avenge Myself on My enemies." (Isaiah 1:24). Nothing in the verse says to wait. He says He will avenge Himself.
Sending them away isn't in this verse, friend. The Lord GOD of Hosts says, "…avenge Myself on My enemies." (Isaiah 1:24). He names avenging, not relocating. That's the answer.

Not quite, friend. The Lord says, "I will thoroughly purge your dross; I will remove all your impurities." (Isaiah 1:25). Thoroughly and all are big words. He doesn't say some, and He doesn't say a few.
That's right, baker. The Lord says, "I will thoroughly purge your dross; I will remove all your impurities." (Isaiah 1:25). He doesn't say some, He says all. No leftover bits get left behind.

Yes, baker. The Lord says, "I will restore your judges as at first, and your counselors as at the beginning." (Isaiah 1:26). Notice the words as at first and as at the beginning. He points back to how it started.

Actually the text says it outright, friend. The Lord says, "I will restore your judges as at first, and your counselors as at the beginning." (Isaiah 1:26). So this one is True. After all that heavy news, here comes some hope.

The verse goes the other way, friend. The Lord says, "After that you will be called the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City." (Isaiah 1:26). The harlot name from verse 21 doesn't stick. So the answer is False.

You've got it, baker. The Lord says, "After that you will be called the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City." (Isaiah 1:26). Back in verse 21 Isaiah calls her a harlot, and here she gets a new name instead. The city gets a good name, and that's the last word on it.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "Zion will be redeemed with justice, her repentant ones with righteousness." (Isaiah 1:27). The ones who turn back are the ones named here. It's a short phrase, but it carries a lot.

Rulers aren't named in this verse, friend. Isaiah says Zion will be redeemed with justice, "…her repentant ones with righteousness." (Isaiah 1:27). The text points to the repentant ones, whoever they are. That's the answer.

Priests don't appear in this passage at all, friend. Isaiah says Zion will be redeemed with justice, "…her repentant ones with righteousness." (Isaiah 1:27). Think about what repentant means: people who turn around. Those are the ones named here.

The text says the opposite, friend. Isaiah says, "But rebels and sinners will together be shattered, and those who forsake the LORD will perish." (Isaiah 1:28). That's a different outcome from the repentant ones in verse 27. So the answer is False.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says, "But rebels and sinners will together be shattered, and those who forsake the LORD will perish." (Isaiah 1:28). The word But marks the turn away from the repentant ones in verse 27. It's a heavy verse, and the text doesn't soften it.

Withered, yes. Isaiah says, "For you will become like an oak whose leaves are withered, like a garden without water." (Isaiah 1:30). Picture a plant that nobody watered, with brown, dried-up leaves. The people delighted in their sacred oaks and gardens, and now they're told what they will become like.

Evergreen would stay fresh, friend, and that's not the picture here. Isaiah says they'll be "…like an oak whose leaves are withered, like a garden without water." (Isaiah 1:30). Withered leaves and a dry garden go together. Withered is the answer.

Spreading sounds healthy, friend, but the verse says otherwise. Isaiah says the people will be "…like an oak whose leaves are withered, like a garden without water." (Isaiah 1:30). Leaves that are withered and a garden without water are the picture he gives. The answer is withered.

The verse says the opposite, friend. Isaiah says, "both will burn together, with no one to quench the flames." (Isaiah 1:31). Nobody is there to put the fire out. I think this is a heavy verse to end on, so the answer is False.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says, "both will burn together, with no one to quench the flames." (Isaiah 1:31). Nobody is there to put it out. I think this is a heavy way to end the passage, so it's good to take it seriously.
